To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of nitrification inhibitor (DCD) is recommended for autumn-applied slurry to reduce winter nitrate losses; (2) the economically optimum rate of spring-applied slurry is lower than the rate of autumn-applied sludge; (3) N fertilizer rates in spring are not related to N crop uptake; (4) the amount of residual soil mineral nitrogen in spring depends on the amount of mineral nitrogen in spring, the crop demand and the amount of rain
the application of nitrification inhibitor DCD to autumn-applied slurry, reduced nitrate losses during the winter period.
the nitrate concentration of ground water can be reduced, by applying slurry and mineral N in spring and by applying slurry in combination with DCD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of slurry and mineral N application on soil and crop, and the effects of N fertilization on nitrate leaching.
the development of a strategy for reducing nitrate leaching from arable land, which takes into account the economic constraints.
a number of issues that need attention when considering N fertilizer management in the context of environmental quality and sustainability of agricultural systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the long run, the nitrate problem can only be solved by a drastic reduction of N inputs, and by a shift from autumn to spring application of cattle slurry.
the effects of nitrification inhibition, time and rate of N application are not straightforward.

the nitrate problem in the sandy soils of The Netherlands is not due to excessive amounts of N applied, but to the fact that a large proportion is lost to the environment, due to high soil mineral N levels and high rainfall in spring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of nitrification inhibitor in autumn-applied slurry, was a promising approach to reduce nitrate losses during the winter period.
the nitrate concentration of groundwater is not determined only by the amount of N applied to the soil, but also by the time and rate of application and the soil type.

, in order to reduce nitrate losses to the environment, N inputs should be limited to the economically optimum rates and slurry applications should be postponed to spring, but also that, in the long-term, a reduction of the livestock numbers is required.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, to reduce N losses to the environment, N fertilization should be based on a combination of N mineralization and crop uptake measurements and on the use of N fertilizers and manure that are less prone to leaching.
, to reduce N leaching, N inputs must be limited, and N fertilizer should be applied at rates below economically optimum levels.

the N fertilizer rate should be reduced to a level where nitrate concentrations in groundwater do not exceed the EC limit for drinking water, and that the N fertilizer should be applied as a split application.
